The risk of cross-resistance to previously used antiretroviral regimens, such as integrase inhibitors, second-generation non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), and protease inhibitors (PIs), is minimal. This recommendation is conditional and based on low-quality evidence. 2. Patients on a failing second-line antiretroviral regimen with no new antiretroviral options available should continue with a regimen that is tolerated. This is a conditional recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 3. For children, strategies that carefully balance the benefits and risks need to be explored when second-line treatment fails. 4. For older children and adolescents who have access to more therapeutic options, constructing third-line antiretroviral regimens using novel drugs, such as etravirine (ETV), darunavir (DRV), and raltegravir (RAL), which are commonly used in adults, may be feasible. 5. Children on a failing second-line regimen with no new antiretroviral drug options should continue with a regimen that is tolerated. 6. Mobile phone text messages can be considered as a reminder tool to promote adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) as part of a broader package of adherence interventions. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 7. In settings with generalized HIV epidemics, ART should be initiated and maintained in eligible pregnant and postpartum women, as well as in infants, within maternal and child healthcare settings. Linkage and referral to ongoing HIV care and ART should be ensured where appropriate. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 8. In settings with a high burden of HIV and tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated for individuals living with HIV in TB treatment settings, with linkage to ongoing HIV care and ART. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 9. In high HIV and TB burden settings, TB treatment may be provided for individuals living with HIV in HIV care settings where TB diagnosis has also been made. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 10. ART should be initiated and maintained in eligible individuals living with HIV in care settings where opioid substitution therapy (OST) is provided. This is a strong recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 11. Decentralization of ART initiation and maintenance should be considered. Options include: Initiating ART in hospitals and maintaining it in peripheral health facilities (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Initiating and maintaining ART in peripheral health facilities (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Initiating ART at peripheral health facilities with maintenance at the community level, such as outreach sites, health posts, home-based services, or community-based organizations, between regular clinical visits (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 12. Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can initiate first-line ART. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 13. Trained non-physician clinicians, midwives, and nurses can maintain ART. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 14. Trained and supervised community health workers can dispense ART between regular clinical visits. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 15. National authorities should implement clinical and operational recommendations using a transparent, open, and informed process. This process should involve broad stakeholder engagement, including meaningful participation from affected communities, and consider the specifics of the recommendations under discussion. 16. Decision-making should take into account national and local HIV epidemiology, current ART program performance, and the socioeconomic, policy, and legal context, including budgetary and human resource requirements and other health system implications. 17. WHO first published guidelines on the use of ART for HIV infection among adults and adolescents in 2002 and on the use of antiretroviral drugs for preventing mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) in 2001 and 2004. Updates in 2006 introduced a public health approach with simplified and harmonized ART regimens. 18. In 2013, WHO revised and combined these and other antiretroviral-related guidance documents into one set of consolidated guidelines addressing the use of antiretroviral drugs for HIV treatment and prevention across all age groups and populations. 19. The consolidated guidelines provide updated, evidence-based clinical recommendations outlining a public health approach to providing ART for HIV treatment and prevention, focusing on settings with limited capacity and resources in the health system. 20. The guidelines also offer guidance on operational and service delivery issues to increase access to HIV services, strengthen the continuum of HIV care, and integrate the provision of ART into health systems. 21. The guidelines are intended primarily for national HIV program managers but are also relevant to clinicians, health service providers, community-based organizations, and international agencies supporting HIV programs in resource-limited settings. 22. The guidelines address clinical, operational, and programmatic aspects of using antiretroviral drugs for HIV treatment and prevention, including HIV testing and counseling, prevention based on antiretroviral drugs, general HIV care, and recommendations on when to start and what ART regimens to use. 23. The guidelines emphasize the importance of timely updates and comprehensive reviews of new science and emerging practices in the use of antiretroviral drugs every two years across populations, age groups, and settings. 24. The guidelines aim to provide programmatic guidance for decision-makers and planners at the national level on adapting, prioritizing, and implementing clinical and operational recommendations and monitoring their implementation and impact.
